questions.q: According to Bostrom, what limits AI progress today?
a: Access to enough data rather than processing hardware
The lack of sufficiently fast processors
A shortage of trained programmers
The high cost of building robots
questions.why: Lesson 1 says hardware is no longer the main constraint; feeding computers enough information is.

questions.q: What held AI back after the 1956 Dartmouth workshop?
a: Hardware could not handle the complex tasks
No useful algorithms had been invented
Governments banned the research
The public showed no interest
questions.why: Lesson 1 says early machines could handle simple problems but lacked the power for complex ones.

a: Copying a human brain's data so a computer can simulate it
Training a computer on recordings of human speech
Building robots with human-like bodies
Linking many computers into one network
questions.why: Lesson 2 describes WBE as simulating rather than merely imitating human thought.

questions.q: Why does Bostrom warn against a secret government program building superintelligence?
a: A single machine would be easy for one set of bad hands to misuse
It would cost far more than a global effort
It would take far longer to develop
It would give ordinary citizens too much power
questions.why: Lesson 3 says if only one unit exists, one malicious actor could wipe out the species and few could fix it.

questions.q: What makes global collaboration the safer route to superintelligence?
a: Many parties and the public can oversee safety as it develops
It guarantees the technology arrives sooner
It keeps individual countries from learning the details
It removes the need for any regulation
questions.why: Lesson 3 says an open, shared effort builds safety rules along the way, even if it moves more slowly.
